ululate.e: Borrowed from Latin ululō, ululātus, of imitative origin. Cognate with Spanish aullar (“to howl”) and ulular (“to hoot”), and French ululer (“to howl”).

s.d: emit long loud cries
x: wail in self-pity
howl with sorrow

s.d: To howl loudly or prolongedly in lamentation or joy.
x: Women dance in tight circles, ululating with joy, while groups of men sit nearby watching.

s.d: To produce a rapid and prolonged series of sharp noises with one's voice.

ululation.e:
]
Borrowed from Latin ululātiō, from ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”) (from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root) + -ātiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)). By surface analysis, ululate + -ion.

s.d: a long loud emotional utterance
x: he gave a howl of pain
howls of laughter

s.d: The act of ululating; a long, loud, wavering cry or howl.
x: The overthrown Martian set up a prolonged ululation, and immediately a second glittering giant, answering him, appeared over the trees[.]
As we started there broke from the thick silent woods behind us a sudden great ululation of the ape-men, which may have been a cheer of triumph at our departure or a jeer of contempt at our flight.
